title: Just Four Weeks on a Vegan Diet Can Shift Genes Linked to Inflammation and Aging, Study Finds
excerpt: A UC San Diego study found measurable epigenetic changes in healthy adults after one month on a plant-based diet — findings that echo the vegetarian traditions long practiced across the Indian subcontinent
body:
• A randomized clinical trial by UC San Diego and University of Freiburg researchers found that switching to a vegan diet for just four weeks produced measurable changes in DNA methylation patterns linked to reduced inflammation and slower biological aging.
  • The 48 healthy adults in the study showed shifts in immune cell composition, with the vegan group developing a less inflammatory immune profile and showing deceleration on two biological aging clocks.
  • The vegan diet also appeared to reduce activity in cancer-related gene pathways and promote changes linked to lower cholesterol, improved insulin response, and enhanced DNA repair.
  • The findings build on a landmark 2023 Stanford identical-twins study that showed similar anti-aging epigenetic benefits from an 8-week vegan diet.

Switching to a fully plant-based diet for as little as one month can produce real, measurable changes in how your genes behave — shifting molecular patterns associated with inflammation, metabolism, and biological aging, according to a new study published in the journal MedComm.

Researchers at the University of California, San Diego and the University of Freiburg in Germany randomly assigned 48 healthy adults to follow either a vegan diet or a meat-rich diet for four weeks after an initial week on a standardized baseline diet. Both groups consumed similar calories, allowing the team to isolate the effects of food composition rather than weight loss.

The Epigenome Responds Quickly

The researchers analyzed more than 800,000 sites across the genome where DNA methylation — a process that turns genes on or off without altering the DNA code itself — takes place. The vegan group showed distinct changes in methylation patterns that corresponded to a less inflammatory immune state: lower proportions of inflammation-driving neutrophils and higher proportions of CD4 T cells, which help regulate immune response.

Two established epigenetic aging clocks designed to predict health outcomes suggested participants on the vegan diet experienced a deceleration in biological aging over the one-month period.

"Our genes are not our destiny. The epigenome responded measurably in just four weeks, showing that our biology is far more dynamic — and responsive to everyday choices — than we often assume."

— Jerome Mertens, PhD, UC San Diego School of Medicine

Cancer Pathways and Metabolic Benefits

Beyond inflammation and aging markers, the vegan diet appeared to reduce activity in genes involved in cancer-related pathways and promote epigenetic changes linked to lower cholesterol, improved insulin sensitivity, and enhanced DNA repair response. Lead researcher Lukas Karbacher noted that the methylation-based estimates closely matched actual blood-cell measurements taken during the trial.

"That agreement told us we weren't just seeing changes on a computer screen — we were detecting real and meaningful biological changes," Karbacher said.

Building on the Stanford Twins Study

The findings echo results from a landmark 2023 study conducted at Stanford University involving 22 pairs of identical twins. In that 8-week trial, twins randomized to a vegan diet showed improvements in biological aging markers, lower LDL cholesterol, lower fasting insulin, and beneficial gut microbiome changes compared to their omnivorous siblings.

"We are not surprised by these recent findings, and are pleased to see that the types of findings we got in our study are being replicated in other studies," said Christopher Gardner, director of nutrition studies at the Stanford Prevention Research Center.

A Natural Fit for Indian Dietary Traditions

The research carries particular resonance for the Indian diaspora, where vegetarian and plant-forward diets have been a cultural and religious practice for centuries. India has the world's largest vegetarian population, with an estimated 30 to 40 percent of the country following a vegetarian diet — a tradition rooted in Hinduism, Jainism, and Buddhism.

While the study focused on fully vegan diets rather than lacto-vegetarian traditions common in South Asia, the findings add scientific weight to the long-held belief that reducing animal products from the plate carries tangible health benefits. Researchers cautioned that the study was small and short-term, and that larger, longer trials are needed to determine whether these epigenetic changes translate into lasting health improvements.
